TextBlock.TextLine: INTRODUCTION

While
certain
types
of
vertebrate
muscle
have
been
intensely

studied ,
relatively
little
work
has
been
conducted
on
fish
muscle .

Work
done
show
several
distinct
peculiarities
of
fish
muscle
compared

to
typical
vertebrate
muscle
( e.g. ,
amphibian ,
mammalian ) .
Higher

teleost
muscle
( including
the
sand
dab's
family ,
Acanthopterygi )

utilizes
an
unusual
type
of
fast
fiber
innervation .
Each
fast
fiber

is
multiply
innervated
( Barets ,
1961 ;
Hudson ,
1969 ) ,
not
focally
like

most
other
vertebrate
fast
muscle .
This
type
of
fast
muscle
innervation
However ,

has
been
previously
reported
only
in
lower
vertebrates .

multiple
innervation
is
usual
for
vertebrate
non - action
potential

producing
slow
fibers .
In
lower
vertebrates ,
multiply
innervated

fibers
are
slow
and
are
used
primarily
for
posture
( Peachey ,
1961 ) ,

while
in
higher
vertebrates
such
muscles
have
very
specialized
function

( e.g. ,
extraocular
and
middle
ear
muscles )
( Bach - y - Rita
and
Ito ,
1966 ) .

Fish
muscle
is
claimed
further
atypical
for
vertebrates
because
fish

muscles
studied
thus
far
lack
sensory
organs
known
as
muscle
spindles .

Only
a
handful
of
electrophysiologic
studies
have
examined
fish

fast
fibers .
Most
studies
have
found
that
muscle
action
potentials

are
characterized
by
overshoots
close
to
0
mV
or
by
failure
to
overshoot .

Spikes
typically
appear
as
graded
regenerative
responses
and
are
not

all - or - none
( Hagiwara
&
Takahashi ,
1967 ;
Hidaka
&
Toida ,
1969 ;
Hidaka
&
Kuriyama ,

and
Barets ,
1961 ) .
Other
vertebrate
fast
fibers
do
show
overshooting ,

all - or - nothing
action
potentials .
Additionally ,
few
studies
have

investigated
properties
of
isometric
contraction
in
these
fast
fibers .

Of
a
limited
sampling
of
muscles ,
seahorse
fin
muscle
is
reported
as

one
of
the
fastest ,
with
an
isometric
contraction
time
as
short
as

10
ms
to
peak ,
and
shows
a
fusion
frequency
of
120
Hz
( Bone ,
1978 ) .
